slides: So far we've finished lines, angles and triangles. Now let's look at quadrilaterals, shapes with four sides. We'll start with a general one.

slides.say: A quadrilateral is a closed shape with four sides. Here are four points. Let's join them. One side, two, three, and four, back to where we started. The shape is closed, and it has four sides, so it's a quadrilateral.

slides: Its sides don't have to be equal, and its angles don't have to be right angles. If the question doesn't say so, don't add it yourself.

slides.say: Here are two more quadrilaterals. They look different, but each one is closed and has four sides. And here are two shapes that are not quadrilaterals. This one has four sides, but its ends don't meet, so it isn't closed. And this one is closed, but it has five sides.
A quadrilateral can also look like this. Its angles don't all have to be smaller than a hundred eighty degrees. One angle can even be bigger than a hundred eighty, like the angle at C here.

Now the sum of the angles in a quadrilateral. Here's a quadrilateral, A B C D. Let's draw a diagonal, a line from B to D. It splits the quadrilateral into two triangles.

We know that the angles in a triangle add up to a hundred eighty degrees. So the three teal angles of triangle A B D add up to a hundred eighty. And the three orange angles of triangle B C D add up to a hundred eighty too.

Now look at the corners of the quadrilateral. The angles at A and at C are whole. The angles at B and at D are each made of a teal piece and an orange piece. So all the pieces together are exactly the four angles of the quadrilateral. A hundred eighty plus a hundred eighty is three hundred sixty.
